en: *(n0. 5605 gha)* (Title: *Kaulārcanadīpikā* [The Lamp of Kaula Worship] from the *Śrījñānatantra*) (Author: Totakaula)
(Extent: 104 folios) (Date: Saṃvat 1947) (Subject: Tantraśāstra; complete)
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Oṃ, salutations to the Supreme Deity. Oṃ, salutations to the Lamp of the Kula. Oṃ!

That evil-minded person who, disregarding the Kula-dharma, practices the scriptures of the unenlightened (paśu), is like one who leaves the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in his own house and wanders about seeking food elsewhere. (1) Having abandoned [the true path], he roams...
He who, though belonging to the Yakula dharma, becomes devoted to the dharma of cattle, being afflicted by thirst like one at a pond, runs after a mirage.
(2) Neither out of greed, nor anger, nor hatred, nor envy, nor desire, nor fear should one ever abandon the Yakula dharma. (3)
O Beloved, one who lacks knowledge of the lineage is lower than even a dog-cooker (*śvapaca*), though he may be learned in the four Vedas;

yet a dog-cooker who possesses knowledge of the lineage excels even a Brahmin. When the Bhairavī-cakra is active, all castes are twice-born (*dvijāti*); when the Bhairavī-cakra has ceased, all castes remain distinct.

He who finds pleasure in that which is devoid of the fragrance of wine and meat is a sinner; he must perform penance, for he is undoubtedly nothing but a beast. (6) Worship performed daily is the highest;
worship performed once a month is mediocre; worship performed once a year is the lowest; and beyond a year, one becomes a beast. (7) [Kāmā...]

In the Khyāta-tantra it is said: "O Lord of Gods, heaps of great sins are destroyed in that very instant by the five principles (*pañcatattva*), just as a mass of cotton is consumed by fire. Wherever the five principles exist, there the Goddess dwells upon the earth; but where she is devoid of the five principles, the Mother of the World turns her face away. (8-9) Ja.

In the Kali age, O Goddess, especially on the island of Jambūdvīpa, there shall be no animal sacrifice, no animal sacrifice, no animal sacrifice by the command of Śiva. There is no alternative rite in the difficult Kali age; there is no alternative rite in the Kali yuga—of this there is no doubt, no doubt, no doubt in the Kali yuga. (10–11)

Just as there can be no sprout from sowing seeds upon a stone, O Goddess, nor indeed can there be cultivation on the earth without rain; just as offspring is not produced by a woman without her season, O Goddess, nor is there attainment of a higher station without spiritual practice.

(13) Therefore, the practice of the Goddess and the five principles (*pañcatattva*) are in vain without [the proper lineage]; having obtained the mantra of Kālī or Tārā, one does not engage in the conduct of a hero (*vīrācāra*). (14) For that very reason, the state of a *śūdra* is attained in his body, and not otherwise; likewise, O Goddess, even a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya attains the status of a *caṇḍāla*.

A Śūdra shall go [to hell] and becomes a pig; of this there is no doubt. O beloved, as there is no sap in a plantain tree or strength in a bamboo stalk, so there is no liberation—there is none, none at all, O beloved. In the *Kuloḍḍīśa*, it is said: "One should never look [upon the deity] except at the time of worship."
One should drink the Śakti who is naked; even if seen, one’s lifespan diminishes, and having drunk [otherwise], one goes to hell.

A Brāhmaṇa may drink liquor during the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice or according to family custom; otherwise, having drunk it out of desire, he certainly incurs mental affliction. This has been stated in the *Rudrajāmala* regarding truth.

In the Kṛta age, the Goddess was worshipped by the four castes with milk, clarified butter, honey, and flour-offerings (19). In the Tretā age, she was worshipped with clarified butter by all classes; in the Dvāpara age, one should worship her with honey by all castes (20). In the Kali age, the Goddess is to be worshipped by the Kula with those very same spirituous liquors alone.

When [the sacrificer] has died, a Brāhmaṇa may drink the *surā* according to the *sautrāmaṇī* ritual and the family tradition; however, having drunk it for any other reason than that, he certainly becomes subject to penance. In this matter also, there is no doubt, as stated in the *Uḍḍīśottara-khaṇḍa*: "But, O child, why does the mind become clear without a cause?"

(22) Bestowed [are these names]: internal purity, purity of mind, how could it be devoid of cause? It is the cause of wine, and its very essence is the supreme nectar. (23) She is the giver of knowledge, the giver of auspiciousness, the sacred ford; she is the intoxicating Madirā, the virtuous one. She is the bestower of the Kula, the Gaṅgā of the Kula, the purifier, and the savior from the ocean of existence. (24)
O delighter of your lineage, know those cowherd girls to be my own names;
meditate upon her who possesses their very nature—intoxicated by me, adorned with a conch shell, and whose face is full of love.
Remember that beautiful-toothed one who bestows auspiciousness, and always behold her with a tranquil mind through your eye. (25-26)

"O child, know that in every age, the practice of giving knowledge has been lost; devoid of its cause, ritual action has perished, as have internal purity and happiness. Know the body to be in vain without my means of attainment (*sādhana*); and know that practice (*sādhana*), O son, is in vain without the discourse on the Cause (*hetuvāda*). Listen. (27-28)

It is certain that the perfection of the Kevala-japa will be attained by one’s son; therefore, being ever joyful, one should always perform the japa of Mahādevī Modinī. Even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin committed throughout many lifetimes are destroyed by a mere drop [of this practice] upon the tongue of Tāriṇī.

(30) These [deities] grant sovereignty and other such powers, as well as the worship of the creeper-like goddesses, the worship of Rati, and liberation; they are the desired object of accomplishment for heroes. (31) Accomplishment (*siddhi*) does not exist without meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), nor does recitation (*japa*) exist without meditative cultivation; there is no cause without meditative cultivation—everything is established upon meditative cultivation.
Therefore, O child, know that devotion—which is the very nature of my own splendor—is the savior from this [suffering].

By taking refuge in it with a mind endowed with devotion, and by practicing the excellent Dharma, O child, these faults indeed do not arise; moreover, many other faults are destroyed through right application.

(34) The curses pronounced here against Brahmā and others of fickle mind have passed away; having extracted [the mantra] by means of this mantra, become intent upon my worship. (35) Know that Goddess, who is my own essential form, to be eternally pure; without her, the mind is always defiled.

One should abandon [the body] (36). When impurity has been abandoned, the mind and body partake of their own true nature; therefore, having resorted to the liquor, perform the practice with diligence (37). It is revealed as unmanifest, most secret, blissful, and the purifier of all. It is made manifest.
Whether it is made manifest or kept hidden, I shall destroy his lineage; he who is devoted to that [lineage] is beloved by the Gaṇas. O Maheśvara, desist from this Uttarakhaṇḍa!
The manifestation of the Kula leads to destruction, while its concealment leads to spiritual perfection (siddhi). Thus indeed...

The auspicious Śiva, who is thus peaceful yet terrifying to the world, spoke: "I bow to you, O Mahākālī; please explain that by which I, deluded and filled with darkness, may be liberated, O Goddess. For those who revile the heretics—" [40-41]... [text truncated] ...may they be destroyed. I am your servant. [42] The Goddess said: "O son, listen attentively to the supreme secret of the *Kulārṇava*. It is not to be told to anyone at all, nor to one who has not been initiated. [43] "O son, this *Kulārṇava* is the best of secrets; it should not be given to one who is not devoted, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Kula*. [44] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Kula*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Guru*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Śakti*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Mantra*. [45] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Mudrā*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Cakra*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Tattva*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Linga*. [46] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Sthāna*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Pīṭha*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Bhūta*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Jñāna*. [47] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Yoga*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Dharma*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Vrata*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Śraddhā*. [48] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Tīrtha*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Puṇya*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Dāna*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Homa*. [49] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Japa*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Dhyāna*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Nyāsa*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Arcana*. [50] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Śauca*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Māna*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Vitta*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Kāla*. [51] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Deśa*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Kṣetra*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Siddhi*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Mukti*. [52] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Ātman*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Paramātman*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Jīvātman*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Viśvātman*. [53] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Brahman*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Viṣṇu*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Rudra*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Maheśvara*. [54] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Sūrya*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Candra*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Agni*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Vāyu*. [55] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Ākāśa*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Pṛthivī*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Apas*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Tejas*. [56] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Vidyut*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Nabhas*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Tāraka*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Graha*. [57] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Nakṣatra*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Rāśi*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Lagna*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Hora*. [58] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Daśā*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Antardaśā*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Pratyantardaśā*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Mahādaśā*. [59] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Varṣa*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Māsa*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Pakṣa*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Tithi*. [60] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Vāra*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Yoga*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Karana*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Lagna*. [61] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Udaya*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Astamaya*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Madhyāhna*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Sandhyā*. [62] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Prātaḥ*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Sāyam*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Madhya*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Rātri*. [63] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Pūrva*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Paścima*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Uttara*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Dakṣiṇa*. [64] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Diś*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Vidiś*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Ūrdhva*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Adhas*. [65] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Bhūmi*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Antarikṣa*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Svarga*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Pātāla*. [66] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Meru*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Kailāsa*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Vaikuṇṭha*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Vaivasvata*. [67] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Indra*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Yama*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Varuṇa*, nor to one who is not a devotee of the *Kubera*. [68] "One should not give it to one who is not a devotee of the *Īśāna*, nor to one who
"By drinking this, I shall become radiant; I shall not be a heretic, O crusher of great heretics!
Without wine there is no accomplishment, without wine there is no mantra, without wine there is no worship; one who lacks wine would be a non-asura. [Without] wine... (43) [Without] wine.
O Śaṅkara, delusion does not depart; I am far from that state of deluded intellect, therefore, O Lord, take refuge in me.
(44) You should always proceed according to the Mahācīna-krama, O Śiva; with a steady mind and tranquility, you must act as a self-restrained ascetic. (45)

First is the drinking of the *kulāmṛta* (the nectar of the lineage); through that, the mind becomes purified. One born of the *kula* is always most excellent, the Lord of all Lords of Yoga. (46) Śrī Śyāma said: O child, it must be hidden, hidden again, hidden, and hidden again and again; from failing to hide it, there is a loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*).

(47) Listen to that which has been told to you— the root knowledge of Bhairava, namely, unity as it is explained further on. (48) Beholding, touching, and looking at a woman with eyes rolling from wine,
perform the recitation (*japa*) alone with an undisturbed mind, [conceiving her] solely in the form of the Mother (*Mātṛ*).

One should behold her with great joy. (49) I alone am the recitation (*japa*) of all forms of knowledge; of this there is no doubt. It is the settled conclusion of the scriptures that liberation is not attained through sexual union in the womb.
(50) The various *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇa* texts have been composed [to this effect].
And for the destruction of the ignorance of living beings, listen, O beloved of life!

One should worship the Yoni, which is the form of supreme bliss and possesses beautiful hair; especially in the Kali Yuga, one should worship that which is the form of the Yoni, consisting of the universe, with the highest Śakti. For him who worships thus... (51-52)

Liberation rests in the hand; the accomplishment of Tāriṇī is not attained without the Cīna-krama. One's own practice within the mantra is considered the supreme service; loss of fruit results from lack of faith, therefore one should be intent upon the true disposition (bhāva). Whatever has been written here in this Tantra regarding the deity—
(55) All this must be performed by practitioners who desire the state of realization within the Niṣaṃjñika [state].

Listen with supreme devotion and, being attentive, comprehend it; it must not be told to anyone at all, even at the cost of one's life—of this there is no doubt—and it should be guarded like one's own womb, O Lord of Gods.

O beloved, I shall declare the truth, the most firmly established truth, which is not hidden: by the mere performance of which one does not sink into the ocean of worldly existence. Mahāmāyā is of the form of the Yoni, and Sadāśiva is of the form of the Liṅga. Therein, [the worship] is performed with semen, with libations, and with the central meats.

O beautiful one, having inserted the *liṅga* into the *yoni*, one should offer everything to the Śakti; by that truth, one should satisfy the Goddess who is the form of the *bhaga* and consists of the universe. O Lord of Gods, by the counter-stroke (*pratyāghāta*), one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin; O Durgā, faith [in this] does not belong to those of little merit.
Among all means of accomplishment, the womb-sacrifice (*yonisādhana*) is certainly born as the supreme;

O Goddess of the gods, if one worships the Yoni after eating and drinking, the sin accumulated over ten million births perishes in that very instant. Through enjoyment one attains liberation; through enjoyment one attains [liberation].
Therefore, with every effort, the practitioner who possesses enjoyments should become happy;

he who always abandons censure, disgust, shame, and pride, and does not worship his own womb during the occasion of family rites—what is the use of his hundreds of thousands of ritual accomplishments? For him, everything is [already attained].
Merely by seeing the *yoni*, one becomes liberated along with ten million lineages;

if one should worship the *yoni* during an eclipse of the moon or sun, performing libations (*tarpaṇa*) with the true nature of the *yoni*, there is no further rebirth. The Goddess resides at the root of the *yoni*, and within the *yoni*.

In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, it is said that whatever is drunk or eaten—whether it be Nāganandinī, Kālī, Tārā, Yonicakrā, Kuntalā, or Chinnamastakā—all that is offered as an oblation into the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī; thus one attains siddhi and is not bound by any fetter. This is alms-food.
"O Mother of Gold, for the sake of my own purpose regarding Kuṇḍalinī, grant me alms; I shall satisfy Kuṇḍalinī.

Abiding in the stage of the Avadhūta and intent upon the bliss of Bhairava, I am Bhairava and there is no other; there is no god higher than I anywhere. [I am devoted to] the Tantra, Mantra, and worship..."
All this has arisen within me and not otherwise; I am Śiva, I am Bhairavānanda, I am the Lord of the Kula.
With limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste, adorned with a red loincloth, wearing red garlands and garments, one should always be endowed with the [proper] cause. Thus, one should wander for alms.
That monk who is intent on terrible conduct is neither diminished by sin nor increased by deceit.

The practitioner of mantra, the Lord of the Kula, should meditate upon himself as having the form of the Goddess. For him, there is no ritual worship, no twilight prayer, no formal observance, and no vow; he is Bhairava, complete in himself.
"I am the one who bestows boons, I am eternal bliss, I am imperishable, adorned with fragrant flower garlands and ornaments of pearls; I am no god superior to another"— thus absorbed in such thought,
the practitioner devoted to his lineage shall partake of the soft substance (mārdaka) as his food.

When agitation arises within me, immovability is produced; therefore, the wise and excellent hero should strive to remain endowed with enjoyment (*bhoga*). Through enjoyment one attains liberation, and through enjoyment one achieves the Kula-sādhana.
Whatever he speaks, whatever he sleeps, whatever he does, and whatever he worships—all that is *Kula*.
Having meditated upon form, the wise one should dwell alone in a desolate place— in a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a forest,
in an empty house, or on a riverbank— and should wander joyfully and without fear. For heroes, the time for recitation is praised as being at all times and in all places.

This must be performed at every sacred seat (pīṭha); of this there is no doubt. Even if a Brahmin has fallen from his status and is devoted to the substances of the *kula*, he should always worship the Goddess even while unwashed and after having eaten. The satisfaction of the *kula* should be performed in a garden or in a secluded place; there is no distinction between a divine (*divya*) and a heroic (*vīra*) [practitioner] in this regard.

The *Sthiryabheda* (the stable type) is described as calm, disciplined, sweet, and endowed with artistic grace and charm; he is divine, resembling a deity, and possesses a heroic mind that is yet exalted.
He is adorned with magnificent ornaments or anointed with sandalwood and other unguents, such as red sandalwood.
Whether he is a Vaiṣṇava or a non-Vaiṣṇava, whether he is an Ārkaragopana or the manifest Kula-bhairava; whether he is unrefined with a mass of hair or refined as Kuleśvara;
whether at times he is disciplined or at times lost, and whether at times he is like a bhūta or piśāca—he remains the same in both insult and honor.

One who is joyful and nourished shall always become so by bowing to and meditating upon a woman— whether she be a child, one intoxicated with youth, an old woman, or likewise a beautiful one, or even a despicable or most wicked one. In the *Uḍḍīśottarakhaṇḍa*, it is said that there is no knowledge superior to this in the three worlds.

Supreme knowledge, which is indeed unity, can never be attained without Vatsatāriṇī; therefore, O Vatsa, she is hidden from all yoginīs. If you perform the ritual in this manner, then at that time, she will certainly manifest herself.
O Śiśaṅkara, this must never be spoken; it must be guarded with great effort.
Devoted to my worship, joined with Śakti upon the bed, and constantly reciting it in the form of supreme bliss, O Digambara, listen, my child, for what I have spoken is indeed the truth.
"O Sadāśiva, through the recitation [of mantras] while naked (digambara), success is attained; of this there is no doubt.

Therefore, O Śiva, by means of the state of non-duality (advaitabhāva), you must always be one who beholds my form day and night during the recitation. [This is stated] in the venerable Ācārasāra-tantra regarding bathing and other rites."

Mental recitation (*japa*), mental worship (*pūjā*), and mental offerings such as libations (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth, do not require external purification; they are always auspicious. There is no time that is inauspicious at any point—neither by day nor by night, nor during the twilights or the dead of night. [This applies even when] regarding clothing...
One should not perform purification here regarding the seat, the house, the body, touch, water, and so forth;

rather, one should practice with a mind free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). Here there is no requirement for purification and the like, nor is there any defect such as impurity. One should always worship the Goddess, whether unwashed or having already eaten. Mahā...

At night, in a pure place, one should cause the bali offering to be given with the mantra: "Those in whose minds the knowledge of the Kula is revealed by the power of fortune, they are to be venerated;
they are great-souled ones, they have accomplished their purpose, they are the best among men. In their minds, the knowledge of the Kula arises through me."
Behold those deluded by the scriptures who, having been terrified by me in the form of a serpent, do not recognize their own family dharma;
they are merely conceited with false knowledge. Indeed, all those animal scriptures were spoken by me alone through another form and through mantras, for the purpose of deluding the wicked-minded.

Due to the power of great sins, a longing for those [lower births] arises in men; indeed, for them there is no auspicious state even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. However, he who, having entered the circle of the womb, mutters the *mūlavidyā*, attains perfection within six months, even without fire-offerings or worship.

If, by the power of fortune, the *yoni-mudrā* of the Goddess is beheld by the gods, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground and perform mental recitation (*japa*). The Great Goddess is of the form of the *bhaga*, and the Yoginī is of the form of the *yoni*; therefore, the knower of mantras should diligently [worship] that Great Mudrā.

One should offer liquor, fish, meat, and likewise honey; a practitioner of the Kula-Kaula path should consume these family substances. Having touched the maiden of the Kula, he should be devoted to the Kula-worship. To her, wine should be given, as well as food and the like.

Having entered the vulva of his beloved, he should recite the mantra with one-pointed mind; regarding himself as Bhairava and the vulva as the Goddess, and being perfected in the conduct of Bhairava, he should enter the circle of the vulva. That Śakti who resides there is the Great Goddess, whose nature is pure bliss.

"O Goddess, having realized that he is not a human being born from that same womb, but is rather a perfected Siddha, a Sādhaka, and a favorite of the Vīras, one should recite the Vidyā while being solely intent upon the Bhāva. If the Sādhaka possesses a notion of caste-connection, he shall never [attain success];
O Goddess, due to that notion of caste-connection, he falls into hell. [The mantra] ucchiṣṭam..."
One should give to women from one's own portion; indeed, one should not give what remains [from others]. One may drink the substance remaining from the Śakti, and chew that which remains from Śiva.
By the grace of the Śakti and the Vīra, what on this earth cannot be accomplished? In the Yonitantra, having placed the mantra of the Śakti before oneself, he who indeed fills the Yoni...
Who is truly fortunate? Who is wise? Even the omniscient Brahmā, with his four faces, is unable to describe him even in hundreds of millions of kalpas, along with all the gods and asuras;
so what is the use of much further talk? If, indeed, by the power of fortune alone, he...
One would attain the womb of the Ṣpā; likewise, having performed the great worship, one would obtain liberation.

Having brought a woman who is free from pity, shame, and modesty—whether she be one's own beloved or another’s supreme beloved—and having placed her in beautiful attire within the mandala, [one should worship] Vijayā in the first [position].

Having placed her upon his left thigh, he should worship with a spirit of devotion that slender-waisted woman with flowing tresses. He should offer sandalwood paste into the cavity of the *yoni* and beautiful flowers;
in this rite, there is no invocation (*āvāhana*), nor the placement of the vital breaths (*jīvanyāsa*), nor the mantra. The cause for this lies in her very mouth.

Having applied sindūra in the shape of a crescent moon on her forehead with sandalwood paste, and having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over both her hands while they rest upon her breasts, O fair-faced one, he should perform the crushing of the breasts in their midst,
preceded by the kissing of the *huṇḍa*, or likewise one hundred and eight times.
Having recited the mantra one thousand times within the *yoni-maṇḍala*, one should chant the hymn endowed with devotion.

By the mere sight of the *yoni*, one obtains the fruit of ten million holy places (*tīrtha*). Even if the practitioner himself sees, touches, or is touched by a woman in her menses, [he should recite] one hundred and eight times...
Having recited that, one becomes a lord of the earth and cities; one should recite the mantra at all times and always within the supreme source (parayoni).
One should worship the Goddess with the thought that she is the Goddess herself; for she is sin personified as Śakti.
One who seeks virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation shall obtain the fruit of the four aims of life (caturvarga); this is not so for those who are merely seekers of worldly enjoyment.
The yogi who possesses song and so forth is indeed not a possessor of enjoyment; he is a Kaula whose nature consists of both enjoyment and liberation if he worships this *yoni*.
O Durgā, without the worship of the *yoni*, all other worship becomes in vain.
For within the *yoni* resides the principal one, the leader of the host of Cāṇḍālas.

By the mere act of worshipping her, one becomes equal to me; of this there is no doubt. How can that wicked soul chant the mantra of Śakti, he who feels no revulsion for sin, for sexual intercourse, or for the drinking of blood and semen, and who possesses delusion and a sense of duality toward the virtuous?

There, the lord of practitioners, united with Śakti, should remain as Maheśvara. O Lord of Devas, all rites such as japa and the like must be performed in the great conch. O Goddess, whatever a man performs without the five principles (pañcatattva), all that is fruitless for him, and in the end he goes to hell.

O Maheśvarī, if one does not worship the very source of the bliss of Mahāvidyā, his mantra will not be perfected even by a hundred *puraścaraṇa* rites. By offering three handfuls of flowers into the cavity of the *yoni*, the merit of his worship for thousands of future births is produced.

O ascetic, the Guru is indeed Śiva himself, and his wife is his very own form. Merely by having sexual intercourse with her, a Kaulika would become a denizen of hell. [The best of practitioners] should crush that which is common to all. Śrī Pārvatī said: By what rite?
The venerable Śrī Śiva, who is the source of the womb, the form of the universe, and the embodiment of power, said:

"Having extracted that Liṅga, one should worship her who is the form of Śakti; Mahāmāyā is in the form of the Bhaga, and Sadāśiva is in the form of the Liṅga. Merely by worshipping these two, one becomes liberated while living; of this there is no doubt."

O Dear One, if one cannot worship with flowers, offerings, and all other requisites due to some difficulty, then one should worship that deity even with the mantra alone; likewise, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) in the "womb" of the womb-mantra (yonimudrā), along with the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the mantra.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred times at the base of the *yoni*, one should wipe the *yoni* upon the *liṅga*. This is proclaimed as the most excellent of all spiritual accomplishments (*sādhana*). O Lord of Gods, this Tantra must never be disclosed; it should not be given to the disciples of others, and especially not to one's own disciples who have not been properly initiated. Bathing...

O Lord of Gods, if at any improper time one should behold the *yoni*, the life of that practitioner is certainly fruitful. Afterwards, in its absence, one should worship the mere *yoni* alone; by the mere worship of the *yoni*, Viṣṇu himself is present—of this there is no doubt—in heaven.

Even as a mortal, he is to be worshipped by gods and demons alike; if, having fully mastered the essential principles (*tattva*), he enters into battle, O Lord of Gods, he will undoubtedly be victorious in the fray. Is it through merely bathing in the Gaṅgā, or by resorting to other sacred pilgrimage sites?

"O Lord of Gods, without devotion to the womb, everything becomes futile; even with five faces, one is not able to describe the greatness of the womb. Listen, O Naga-nandini, for it is by the grace of your womb that the state of Mahadeva was attained."

That practitioner who crushes the womb of fresh Kutnalā is liberated from the great suffering of the terrible ocean of saṃsāra. Is she worshipped by the lord of practitioners merely by bathing in the Gaṅgā, or by resorting to other sacred fords? She is indeed the form of Bhaga herself.
O beloved, what is the use of speaking much more here? Listen, O lotus-faced one:

the worship of the virtuous is common to all, O dear one. Without the five principles (*pañcatattva*), O Goddess, the fourth [principle] becomes fruitless. One should drink the substance remaining from the *śakti* and chew it together with the hero (*vīra*).

Having formed the *mahāyoni* mudrā and having worshipped [the deity] day and night, O Maheshani, one may roam upon the circle of the earth after eating and drinking; wearing a garland of *tulasī*, one should build a temple for Hari and engage in storytelling and the chanting of the virtues of Śrī Hari.

One who has not developed devotion through the name of Hari should dwell in the company of animals; for worship that is more secret than secret results in loss when performed openly. O Pārvatī, worship should not be performed in the presence of an animal;
if one were to worship the yoni after offering three handfuls of flowers, [the result would be ruin].

In the three worlds, there are no actions for him that cannot be performed; depending upon the food of all beings, his eating consists of nectar. O Maheśānī, sexual union is always praised by all yogis. O Durgā, he who is composed of eternal bliss shines forth as a hero.

I shall explain the entire sādhana for attaining omniscience: bathing and so forth are mental; purity is mental; the power of recitation (japa) is mental; the preliminary rite (pūjā) is mental; the divine libation (tarpaṇa) and other such acts are mental; indeed, everything is auspicious—no inauspicious time exists anywhere.

There is no distinction between day and night, nor at the twilights or during the dead of night; even regarding clothing, seats, bathing, the house, the body, touch, and so forth, one should not practice purification there. One should move with a mind free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). There is no restriction of direction or time, nor likewise any restriction regarding standing and other postures.
There is no fixed rule regarding the time for recitation (japa), even when there is no worship or offering of bali. One must never harbor hatred toward women;

indeed, the worship of women is especially meritorious. Wherever the practitioner may go, whether approaching, touching, or looking at a woman, he should offer her edible food and then recite the mantra. As for the edibles, they may be according to his preference; this is his own choice.

The rule prescribed for the rite of *vīrasādhana* is as follows: women are the gods, women are the life-breaths, and women alone are the ornament. One must always remain attached to women; otherwise, one is not even [fit] with one's own wife. This which has been declared in the *Bhāvasarvasva*, hidden in all the *tantras*, concerns the consumption of substances.

One should offer [the substance] with one's power (*śakti*) upon a bed of leaves and so forth; or else, having first cast a portion into the midst of water, the practitioner, endowed with power, should go to the cremation ground at dawn, consume the substance, recite the mantra, and after reciting it, engage in sexual union (*maithuna*).
What is the use of hundreds of thousands of divine means?

O Maheśānī, what is the use of serving one's own *mūlādhāra* and other centers, or what is the use of hundreds or lakhs of worship, charity, or even austerity, without the *bhaga*? All of it becomes utterly futile.
Merely by worshipping the *yoni*, one partakes in the fruit of all spiritual practices; indeed, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) offered to the reality of the *yoni* [yields the same].
One who desires to go to heaven should always fondle the womb [of the disciple] by means of pulling her hair and other such acts.

O Maheśānī, if one places [the disciple] upon one's lap and performs the *vāgbhava* [mudrā], then, liberated from the sins accumulated since birth, he is released along with ten million lineages. [Likewise for] the womb of a female disciple...
One should especially worship the source of incense (Dhūyoni) with a state of pure devotion using perfumes and flowers;

having enjoyed happiness in this world, one is glorified in the world of the Goddess. O Queen of Gods, at the time of worship, if anyone should come here, one should indeed show them the Vaiṣṇavī mudrā according to the ritual of Viṣṇu.
If one should go to Rājagṛha taking with him a stalk of *yonikuntala* grass while reciting this praise,

all his undertakings will undoubtedly succeed through that effort. I, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the sages of pure intent— all creatures within the egg of Brahmā (*āṇḍa*), from the highest heaven down to the lowest abyss— reside in the womb.
O Goddess, who in the three worlds knows the greatness of this Yoni-tattva? Without the five principles— namely honey, meat, fish, mudrā,
and sexual union— everything becomes fruitless, even if one should, by the power of fortune, obtain the sight of a Kaula.

Having gratified him with various kinds of food and edibles, one should entreat him with great effort: "Come, O best of practitioners, you who are devoted to the worship of the *yoni*. By the mere sight of you, I am fulfilled;
of this there is no doubt. [And one should speak thus] during conversation with the animal and in the company of the animal. If [this occurs], then...

O Mahādevī, one who is intent on beholding the *yoni* [will become pure] by means of the *tilaka* [applied] as the *yoni*. O Durgā, the worship of the maiden (*kumārī*) and likewise the feeding of those of noble family (*kulīna*)—these two are certainly the primary elements in this scripture. Internally [she is] Śakti; externally...

In the assembly, Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas, assuming various forms, wander upon the earth as Kaulas. O Daughter of the Mountain, that family in whose lineage one is born after thousands of previous births should be known as noble and pure; [so too is] that place where the washing of feet [takes place].
If one who is sluggish performs [these acts], his body and his home fall into endless [suffering];

even the splendor in the hand of such a beast becomes entirely fruitless. Furthermore, it is impossible for me to describe the greatness of one born of noble lineage; yet those of noble lineage are indeed virtuous.

I have been liberated along with ten million lineages; by the yoga of the Kula alone, I am pleased, of this there is no doubt. O Goddess, among the four stages of life (*āśrama*), the stage of the *avadhūta* is the greatest.
Therein, through the yoga of the Kula, I attained the state of Mahādeva. [The Self...]

If the supreme practitioner, due to some distinction regarding the source [of his lineage], is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells until the dissolution of all beings, yet if he is devoted to the Goddess who exists in the form of Śakti,
then he lives a truly lived life together with ten million of his kin.
Having worshipped her with water for washing the womb and for rinsing the *liṅga*,
one should offer the *arghya* to the Great Yoni according to the prescribed rite. Then, having divided that water into three parts,
the practitioner should present one portion to the Śakti and two portions to the Kāraṇa.
Having mixed it together as established, the best of practitioners should drink it with the Great Goddess.
In the *Kulārṇava*, it is said: "Brahmā is in the mouth, Viṣṇu is in the water, Rudra is in the fragrance, and the Supreme Self is in its juice;
because of that bliss, this should be consumed, O Beloved—even in the absence of meat."
One should worship the Goddess after taking *asuta*, *ārdraka*, or *nāgara*; otherwise, it shall be fruitless. One should satisfy her with liquor even when devoid of fish, meat, and the like;
one must not perform the worship without substances such as fish and meat.

By offering even a mere measure of flesh, or half a sesame seed, or a drop of honey as a single libation, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices. There is no other merit equal to the Kula-pūjā in the three worlds; therefore, he who worships with devotion shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

O Sovereign of the four castes and the four stages of life, he who is a worthy recipient, though unlearned, yet knows the scriptures, is devoted to his guru, firm in his vows, and delights in honoring his family— such a person shall be most dear to Me,
whether he be male, female, or neuter.
O Sadāśivā, when worshipped, you grant the fruits of this world and the next, like a virtuous wife;

but when not worshipped, O Mistress of Gods, you bestow suffering, like a wicked wife. O Goddess, that evil-minded person who performs these rites without the worship of the lineage (Kula-pūjā) shall go to the terrible twenty-first hell.
Therefore, with every effort, one should be devoted to the worship of the *kula*;

one obtains all supernatural powers (*siddhis*), and there is no need for hesitation in this matter. Whatever fruit one might obtain by performing the sixteen great gifts (*mahā-ṣoḍaśa-dāna*), that same fruit one attains by performing [this worship].

Whatever fruit a mortal may obtain by bathing at three and a half crores of sacred fords (*tīrthas*), that same fruit he attains by beholding the *Śrīcakra*. O Goddess, what is the use of much speaking?
He who, according to his devotion, gives *kuladravya* (sacred substances) to the *Kulācārya* for the purpose of worship, [attains] that merit.
Those who, with devotion, offer meat and wine from both hands and thereby produce bliss— those Kolikas are dear to us. Our supreme form,
characterized by pure consciousness and bliss, manifests through the enjoyment of the *kuladravyas* (substances of the lineage), and not otherwise.

The inner radiance of experience is beyond the reach of mind and speech; it arises through the enjoyment of the *kuladravya*, O Beloved, and not otherwise. When the *kuladravya* is consumed, those who perceive the true meaning of the *kula-tattva* become possessed by Bhairava and behold equality everywhere. [Darkness...]

Just as a house covered [by darkness] is seen by means of a lamp, so too the Self, though veiled by illusion, is seen through the drinking of the substance (dravya). O Dear One, those people who drink the family-substance (kuladravya) purified by mantra and worshipped for the sake of the Guru and the Deity, for them there is no longer the need to drink mother’s milk. Indeed, liquor is Bhairava himself.
Vomada is declared to be Śakti; when both are consumed, they delude even the gods.

Having drunk that *maireya* wine, a man who strives in yoga becomes solely intent on true meditation, and he is liberated; he is a *Kaulika*. Wine is Śakti, meat is Śiva, and their consumption is [the union].
When Bhairava has been awakened by himself and their unity has arisen, that which is produced is indeed called bliss (*ānanda*);
bliss is the form of Brahman, and it is established within the body. Liquor (*madya*) is its manifestor;
therefore, it is drunk by yogis who are free from hesitation, fearless, steadfast, and free from dualism.

Free from curiosity and having determined the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, one should drink the boon-granting Varuni wine, which has been purified by the consecration of mantras. O beautiful one, through the drinking of this nectar, the state of divinity arises, which liberates one from the bonds of worldly existence. This should always be drunk by a Brahmin; for a Kshatriya, it is [to be drunk] from the battlefield.

For a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, when drinking wine or eating meat during other ritual acts— after having worshipped the gods and ancestors according to the path prescribed by the scriptures and while remembering the Guru—
one incurs no fault. Indeed, for the sake of the satisfaction of all the gods and for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman, I partake [of these].

If one drinks wine or eats meat out of craving, he is a sinner; however, for the sake of the manifestation of the meaning of the mantra, for the stability of the mind, and for the purpose of severing the bonds of worldly existence, one may practice the drinking of wine.
But he who consumes wine and such things merely for the sake of pleasure is a sinner; [only] should one partake [of them] for the gratification of the deity.

One who is devoid of longing, having not performed the mantra-satiation for the formidable Lord Aṣṭabhairava, even a hero, having drunk according to the rite of animal-liquor, shall go to hell. [The liquor] produced from honey and flowers,
or that produced from rice— whose bliss is changeless and whose fragrance is pleasing to the mind...

O Goddess, this pair of Amṛtānanda is the cause of delight for the gods and deities; by merely smelling its fragrance, one obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices (Śatakratu). By its mere contact, one obtains the fruit of ten million holy places (tīrtha-koṭi). O Goddess, by drinking it, one directly attains liberation.

The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) resides in the joy of the liquor; the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) in its flavor; the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) in its tasting; and the Supreme (*Parā*) resides in its manifestation. In sacrifices to the ancestors, gods, and others, the Veda prescribes violence; however, the killing of living beings for one's own sake [is forbidden] at any time.

One who has renounced the pleasant and unpleasant should never cut even a blade of grass. Having offered [oblations] for the sake of the deities or for the sake of the twice-born, one is not tainted by sins. One may drink water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) that has not been consecrated, and engage in sexual intercourse through force;
however, having eaten meat killed by one's own beloved, one shall go to the Raurava hell. [From] heaven...

Just as there is no difference among the gods in the worlds of merit, so too within the Wheel (cakra) are all deities and all humans; there is no distinction of caste in this Wheel, for all are remembered as equal to Śiva.
Indeed, the Veda declares that everything thus established is Brahman.
What is the use of saying more here? O Mistress of the Kula, within the center of the wheel, men are remembered as my own form and women as your own form.
O Leader of the Kula, the yoginīs devour that deluded soul who, within the center of the wheel, creates distinctions based on caste; I swear this by you.

O fair lady, I am not satisfied even with thousands of jars of wine or hundreds of loads of meat, without the nectar of the bhaga and the liṅga. This world is marked neither by the cakra, nor by the lotus, nor by the vajra; it is marked by the liṅga and the bhaga. Therefore, [I am] Śakti and Śiva.

The union of Śiva and Śakti, which occurs at that time, is the *saṃdhyā* (twilight) perceived by those established in the Kula who abide in samādhi. A lustful man approaching a woman who is desirous, unashamed, purified by immediate consecration (*saṃskāra*), and duly prepared— [this is the state].

One should approach a woman; worship performed daily is the highest, worship on festival days (parvan) is middling, and worship once a month is the lowest, O Goddess. Beyond a month, one becomes like a beast. One should perform worship with prescribed substances such as liquor, meat, fish, and mudrā beyond the month.

The wise one should, according to the prescribed rite, worship the five *makāras*—which bring delight to the deities of the directions—and the five beginning with *mā* (liquor), for the pleasure of the deity Īśāna;
yet if he pursues them out of craving, he is a sinner, and his drinking is as futile as the killing of a hero (*vīrahatyā*). O Hero!

The theft of property, sexual intercourse with the wife of a *vīra*, and association with such persons— this is declared to be the fifth *mahāpātaka* (great sin) in the lineage of the Kaulikas. O Goddess, one should not worship with only one hand, nor drink with only one hand, [using] fish, meat, and fermented liquors.
One should not perform worship in the presence of those who are like bound souls (paśu); rather, having prostrated, one should enter the circle (cakra) and exit after prostrating again.
Those who sit upon the same seat, eat from the same vessel, or drink from the same cup—O Beloved, they go to hell. One should act with a pure mind in the midst of the circle.
That deluded soul who performs washing and other such acts [within the Śrīcakra] shall become a vessel for calamities;
he who emits spittle, impurity, urine, or downward wind into the center of the Śrīcakra becomes a beast for the Yoginīs; and he who engages in jesting or idle chatter [therein]...

One should avoid excessive talk, indifference, fear, and anger in the midst of the ritual circle (*cakra*). One should not touch the vessel with the lotus-hand (*padmī*), nor let a drop fall to the ground. O Dear One, [the offering] should not be given with only one hand, nor without the ritual mudrā. One should not shake the vessel, nor should one make noise therein.

One should not drink liquor from a mixed vessel nor with noise, and likewise one should not fill it to the brim. O Mahādevi, having churned the great ocean of the Vedas and Āgamas with the staff of knowledge, the family dharma—the essence-knowledge—has been extracted. On one side are all dharmas, sacrifices, and sacred fords.

O Dear One, just as rivers—whether flowing straight or winding—enter the ocean from all sides, so too do the *vrata*s and other observances enter the Kula-dharma; indeed, all *samayas* enter the Kula alone.
Just as the footprints of all living beings are contained within the footprint of an elephant, [so are all paths contained within the Kula].

O beloved, just as all rivers become like the ocean through their union with water, so too does any other observance (*samaya*) become equal to the duty of the *kula* through its connection with the *kula-dharma*.
Just as all [other] rivers are not equal to the immortal river (the Gaṅgā), [so it is with other observances].

Likewise, all conventional rules (*samaya*) are not equal by virtue of their respective family traditions (*kuladharma*). Just as there is a vast difference between Mount Meru and a mustard seed, or between the sun and a firefly, so too is there a great disparity between other conventional systems and this [our] family tradition.
Furthermore, through the study of knowledge (*vidyā*), human beings attain liberation across all philosophical systems (*darśana*).
They obtain [the fruit] in the Kaula tradition immediately, without a doubt. What is the use of saying more here?
Listen, O beloved of my life, O Mistress of the Kula of your feet: there is no dharma equal to the Kaula.
A yogi would not be an enjoyer, nor would an enjoyer be a knower of yoga. Yoga...

The Kaula is of the nature of enjoyment; therefore, O Sovereign of the Kula, in this Kuladharma, for one of supreme intellect, enjoyment becomes yoga itself, sin becomes merit, and even worldly existence leads to liberation.
O Goddess of the Kula, [this applies to] Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and other deities, sages, and rākṣasas.
One should abandon talk of celestial chariots (*vimāna*) and the like, as well as all worldly phenomena and the various doctrines of teachers;
indeed, one should know only the *Kula*, if one desires one's own spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Through the practice performed in previous births, the knowledge of the *Kula* becomes manifest within oneself.

O Goddess of the Gods, without the instruction of mantras, the acquisition of faith, or the teaching of many words, a living being obtains that very same intellect which was cultivated in thousands of previous births; thus, instruction is useless. Furthermore, O Kulīnī, all dharmas are remembered as leading to rebirth.

All those who abide in the Dharma are not remembered as such [merely by that]; rather, for men whose sins have been exhausted through previously performed austerities, charity, sacrifices, pilgrimages, recitations, and vows, the Kaula knowledge shines forth, O Goddess— and I shall explain that to you, for both of us are pleased with him.

Through devotion to the deity and the guru, the knowledge of Kula is revealed to one who is pure-minded, peaceful, virtuous, and a servant of the guru. To the devotee of the most secret [teaching], the knowledge of Kula is revealed— [to him] who [has devotion] toward the illustrious guru, the Kula scriptures, the Kaulika teachings, and that which is dear to Kula.

For one whose devotion is firm, the Kaula knowledge shines forth through pure conduct, such as humility and joy, and through steadfast vows. By the command of the Guru, the great dharma of Kaula knowledge is attained;
by this, one who desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra does so without effort. This is the Kula-dharma.

"Having known this, one is liberated; there is no doubt about it. The Śrī Devī said: "O Kuleśa, O Lord of Yogins, I desire to hear about Yoga and its characteristics. O Ocean of Compassion, tell me the fruit of worshipping those devoted to the Kula. Īśvara said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which I have been asked."
You ask about that; by merely hearing it, yoga is directly revealed.
Meditation is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as gross and subtle:
that which has form is called gross, while that which is formless is subtle, for the purpose of steadying the mind.
Some declare that meditation should be on the gross; however, the mind must be made steady even upon the gross, and likewise steady upon the subtle.

O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate on that which is devoid of hands, feet, belly, mouth, and so forth, which consists of all light, and is partless (*niṣkala*) existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*); it neither rises nor sets.
It neither increases nor diminishes; it shines by itself and illuminates others even without external light.

It is infinite, of the nature of light, accessible only through pure existence (*sattāmātra*), and not perceivable by speech or the self. That meditation, known as Brahman, is practiced when the movement of the vital breath has ceased.

O Goddess, the yogi who is as immovable as Mount Śveta, whose path is the true way for the welfare of others, and who is known as a knower of yoga, is called such because he shines only for his own purpose; that meditation which is like the ocean when the moon has set, being devoid of its own form due to the non-contemplation of anything whatsoever, is prescribed as *samādhi*.
When one's own true nature shines forth and that very reality is self-luminated, one becomes identical with it in that very moment.

In the state between dreaming and waking, one remains as if in a dream; free from the breaths of universal existence, motionless like one who is liberated, the entire collection of the senses is rendered still.

O Kaulika, you who have gone beyond the mind are truly liberated while living; you are called pure. Just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee becomes indistinguishable, so too is the relationship between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). Through the power of meditation, even a crocodile [is transformed].

In the same way, through the power of samādhi, a person becomes one with Brahman; just as butter extracted from milk is no longer the same once it has been cast [into fire], so too is the Self described here as being separated from the guṇas. Just as one standing in dense darkness perceives nothing at all, [so does the Self remain when isolated].
Just as one does not perceive any conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) at the time of closing the eyes, so too it should be at the time of opening them;
such is the characteristic of this meditation. Just as a person perceives the itching of his own body, so too he experiences the entire universe as being of the nature of the Supreme Brahman.

When the nature of the deceased has been understood, O servant, you must go toward that which transcends the qualities (*guṇa*) and their transgressions, together with the lords of mantras. For one who is established in the state of oneness with the Self, his activity is the worship of That;
whatever he speaks is mantra, and whatever he meditates upon is the formless.

When the supreme Self is realized and the identification with the body has dissolved for even a moment, wherever the mind goes, there are states of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). When that supreme Self is seen, the knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut away, and the karmas of this yogi are exhausted.

By means of yoga, one attains the stainless, supreme state that has been reached; even that state of gods and asuras which has been attained is no longer grasped. He who perceives the all-pervading, peaceful, blissful, and imperishable—for him nothing remains to be known or understood once knowledge and realization have been fully attained.

O Goddess, when the Knowable has been attained and established within the heart, there is neither yoga nor concentration; once the Supreme Brahman is realized, what is the use of all the observances? What need is there for a palm-leaf fan when the pure breeze has been obtained? There is no need for the binding of the nostrils.
There is no binding of the nose, for there is no fixed rule; for those who perceive "I am myself," there is no yoga in the lotus posture, nor is there the gazing at the tip of the nose.
Those expert in yoga declare that yoga is the unification of the individual soul (jīva) and the Self (ātman) for those who meditate.
Even if one should have faith for only a single moment and think, "I am immortal," the end of the very great merit resulting from that can never be reached.
He who performs self-reflection for even a moment, thinking "I am Brahman," destroys all his sins just as the rising sun dispels the darkness. [This applies to] vows, sacrifices, austerities, and...
The knower of reality obtains ten million times the fruit that is gained from giving gifts, worshipping the gods, and so forth.

The supreme state is innate; meditation and concentration are middling; recitation and praise are inferior; and fire-offerings and ritual worship are the lowest of the low. The highest [state] is contemplation upon reality.
Meditation on the mantra is superior to recitation; reflection on the scriptures is known to be inferior to that; and reflection on worldly affairs is inferior even to that.
Praise is equal to ten million acts of worship; recitation is equal to ten million praises;
meditation is equal to ten million recitations; and absorption (*laya*) is equal to ten million meditations. Indeed, there is nothing superior to meditation.

The deity is none other than one's own Self; therefore, one should not contemplate another. There is no worship higher than that of the Supreme, nor is there a fruit greater than self-satisfaction. Without mantras and water, without *saṃdhyā*, *japa*, and *homa*, and without ritual offerings (*upacāra*), the yogi should constantly perform austerity (*tapas*) and worship within his own body.

The Lord Sadāśiva is the life-force (jīva) joined with the bracelet; he should discard the "wreath" of ignorance while contemplating with the sense of "I am He. The individual soul (jīva) is Śiva, and the divine Śiva is that very soul alone;
bound by fetters it is called a jīva, and freed from fetters it is Sadāśiva—just as [the grain is freed] from the husk.

O Dear One, just as rice is bound by its husk but becomes grains when the husk is absent, so too one bound by karma is always a living being, while one liberated from karma is Śiva. He is the fire for the Brahmins, the deity in the heart of the wise,
and the image for those of dull intellect who perceive the Self everywhere.
If one is equanimous toward blame and praise, cold and heat, pleasure and pain, enemies and friends; if one is free from joy and dejection, desireless, eternally contented, viewing all with equality,
and has conquered the senses— then that yogi, a knower of the supreme reality, dwells in the body like a traveler in a lodging.

Free from doubt, free from conceptual construction, unstained by the impressions of limiting adjuncts, and immersed in his own innate nature— that yogi is a knower of the supreme reality. Just as the lame, the blind, the poor, the impotent, the insane, and the dull-witted dwell in the presence of Kuleśāna, so too does the yogi.

The lord of yogis, who knows the true reality and is filled with the supreme bliss arising from the five mudrās, beholds the Self by means of the self. O beloved, that bliss which arises for the ignorant through the attachment to wine, meat, and women is, for the wise, liberation; for the unwise, it is a downfall.
He who takes delight in the wine of raw flesh, who is ever intent on right conduct, and who is always free from doubt—
he is called a Kulayogin. Drinking the liquor, eating meat, and devoted to acting according to his own will, he should dwell happily, contemplating the unity of "I" and "This."

He whose mouth is devoid of the fragrance of meat and liquor is a sinner and should be avoided like a sacrificial animal; of this there is no doubt. As long as the scent of liquor remains, he is a mere beast, even if he were Paśupati himself.
Without the scent of meat and wine, one is truly Paśupati; otherwise, in this world, he is but a beast.

The base, the exalted, the supreme among the worlds, and the most degraded—this path of the Kula has been proclaimed by the great-souled Bhairava. What is improper conduct is always proper conduct; what is not to be done is the highest duty; even untruth becomes truth for those of the Kula, O Mistress of the Kula—even that which is undrinkable [is drinkable].

O Kuleśvarī, for the Kaulikas, that which is unfit to be drunk becomes drinkable, and that which is unfit to be eaten becomes indeed edible; even that which is forbidden to approach becomes approachable.
For the Kaulikas, O Kuleśvarī, there is neither injunction nor prohibition, neither merit nor sin, neither heaven nor hell, and even their enemies— [are not enemies].

O Mistress of the Kula, the kings themselves are directly the friends and servants of the Kaulikas; O Mistress of the Kula, all people—whether of pleasant countenance or foul countenance, whether proud or otherwise—protect them and bow down before them.
O Mistress of the Kula, those who would be obstructors or adversaries of the Kaulikas [are likewise subdued].

O Goddess, for the Kaulikas, O Mistress of the Kula, death acts as a physician; heaven itself manifests directly; and union with women becomes merit. O Mistress of the Kula, even those Kaulikas who are ignorant of the truth, impoverished, afflicted by disease, or ruined, flourish exceedingly.
O Beloved, by this which has been spoken, the masters of Kula-yoga are always fully accomplished in their intentions;
no deliberation should be made here. Whether in whatever guise, whether marked by whatever [characteristics], and staying in whatever stage of life (āśrama), the Kula-yogi proceeds as a yogi.
Benefiting men through various guises, they wander this earth with their true nature unknown. One should establish the knowledge of the Self once and for all,
dwelling in the midst of the world like one who is insane, mute, or dull-witted, so that one remains unperceived, like a light in the sky.
O Goddess, just as the movement of the moon and sun in the sky, the course of the stars and the planets,
the flight of birds in the air, and the swimming of aquatic creatures in the water cannot be perceived, even so is the state of the yogis; though they do not exist [as ordinary beings], they speak.
O Beloved Lord of the Kula, even those proficient in the Kulayoga may appear like common folk or ignorant people,
so that people might despise them and not seek their company; they do not speak at all,
acting just as a liberated yogi would, playing like a child, O Lord of the Kula.

One should move about like an insentient object, so that this world may despise one as "I am. Having observed from afar how people behave, the yogi proceeds accordingly; in some places he is refined, in some wicked, and in some like a ghost or a piśāca. Thus the yogi wanders, assuming various guises.

On this earth, for the sake of providing a means of livelihood for the world of yogis, and under the guise of practicing yoga, he sports upon the surface of the world, assuming the form of a king out of compassion. Just as the sun dries up everything and fire consumes everything, so too does the yogi enjoy all desires; yet even so, he is not tainted by sins.
He is smeared by all touches, just as the wind; he is all-pervading, just as space;

and just as one is purified by bathing in every river, so is the yogi always pure. Just as food from the house of a mleccha is pure when placed in the hand of a yogi, so do those who know the Kula tradition conduct themselves, O Lord of Gods.
O Supreme Goddess, that very path upon which the masters of yoga— who are confident, who know that [very] path, and who desire their own welfare— proceed,
is called the "Eastern Path" (pūrvā), for it is there that the sun rises; and wherever an elephant goes, there the path is found.
O Mistress of the Kula, wherever a true Kula-yogi may wander, he follows that very path.

Who is capable of obstructing him—who moves according to his own will, who cannot be made crooked or straight, and whose flow cannot be blocked? Just as the sun, endowed with the power of its mantras, sports [unimpeded].

In the same way, the wise one is not smeared even while playing with the serpents of the senses; they are satisfied with the bliss of cessation, devoted to the scriptures, fond of their lineage, established in knowledge, peaceful, and devoted to me—such are the Kaulikas. They are free from non-existence, anger, hypocrisy, and egoism, and are speakers of truth.

O Lord of Kaulikas, those who are not fickle and do not follow the sway of the senses are truly born into the Kula; when their names are being proclaimed, they experience horripilation and a faltering voice, and a bliss that bends them low—this, O Goddess, has been described as the Lord of Kaulika.
In this world, the Kula-dharma is superior to all other dharmas; it is auspicious.
Therefore, those whose intellects are thus resolved are declared to be the best of Kaulikas.
O Dear One, he who knows the reality of the Kula, who is devoted to the Kula scriptures, and who is properly intent on the worship of the Kula—there is no other Kaulika than him.
Through devotion to the Kula, knowledge of the Kula command (ājñā), and the conduct of the Kula...
One who is pleased by the *kulāvṛta* [tradition],

who is dear to the leader of the *Kaulikas*, who, through the acceptance of the three principles (*tatva*), knows the reality of the meaning of the *Kula* mantras, who is devoted to the deity and the guru, and who is a *Kaulika* purified by peaceful initiation— he is difficult for all to find.
O beloved, one attains merit only through the proper preparation of food that demonstrates the conduct of one's family, and not otherwise.
Whether he be a member of the most virtuous lineage or even a *caṇḍāla*, if he happens by chance to be remembered, seen, saluted, or spoken to— even if he were omniscient— [merit is gained].
O Goddess, whether he be a fool, the most excellent, or even the lowest—wherever one of noble lineage and knowledge resides, there I am with you.
I do not dwell on Mount Kailāsa, nor on Meru, nor on Mandara; O beautiful lady, wherever those of noble lineage and knowledge abide, there I abide.
Even if it be far away, that place must be considered as my home.
O Dear One, wherever people devoted to Maheśvara are to be seen with effort, that place is indeed sacred;

for even if the Leader of the Kula is situated very far away, he is to be seen there, whereas one who is a mere bound soul (paśu), though dwelling nearby, is not to be seen. Wherever there is a knower of the Kula-jñāna, that region is meritorious.
By seeing and worshipping such a worthy vessel, one rescues twenty-one generations of one's lineage.
Beholding a knower of the Kula who remains established in his own being, all the ancestors dance with joy;
they take heart like those longing for a timely rain, thinking, "We shall attain the supreme goal."
O beloved, if a son or grandson born in our families becomes a Kaulika,
that man is indeed fortunate in this world, his sins having been destroyed;
for the Kulacāryas approach him, and the Lord of Kaulikas dwells in the abode of the Kaulika.

O Goddess, the Yoginīs always come together with the Yogins; having entered, they partake of the meal along with the Lord of Kula-yoga, and those ancestors and deities [are satisfied]. Therefore, one should worship with devotion those who are devoted to the knowledge of Kula. O Goddess, having worshipped you, one should not fail to worship your devotees.

O lotus-eyed one, those who are most wicked do not become recipients of your grace; you have accepted the food offering (naivedya) merely by sight, even when it is placed before others. O Goddess, you consume the flavors upon the tongue of your devotee; he who worships your devotee has worshipped me, for I am never satiated.

Therefore, desiring what is dear to me, one should worship only those who are devoted to you; whatever is done for those established in the Kula becomes as if done for the gods. All the gods are fond of the Kula;
therefore, one should honor the Kaulas. I am not pleased elsewhere as I am by such devotion.

O Pārvatī, whatever fruit one obtains from the worship of the lords of the Kaulas— when I am properly honored by the lord of the Kaulas as I am pleased— I shall not describe that fruit here through penance,
charity, sacrifices, or vows; nor through what is given, what is desired, what is offered in sacrifice, what is performed as austerity, what is worshipped, or what is recited.

O Goddess, he who would despise the Kaulika makes the Kaula tradition futile; his home is a cremation ground, and that sinner is the lowest of outcasts. If one enters the Kula [tradition] and yet does not know its dharma and its conduct, having abandoned devotion to the Kula, what [is the use] for him? To anyone else...

O Goddess, that gift which is given [in such a manner] is fruitless, and the giver shall go to hell; it is like water poured into a broken vessel, or like seed sown upon a stone. An offering made with many rays [of light], yet lacking the Kaulika knowledge of reality—whatever one may give according to one's capacity, if it is thus...

O Goddess, that fruit which is described for a lay practitioner out of affection on special lunar days cannot at all be described here. O Goddess, having summoned this Kula-knowledge on an auspicious day,
one should worship it with devotion, regarding it as the deity itself, using perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth, along with the five mudrās.
One should satisfy them; when they are satisfied, I am satisfied, and all the deities shall be satisfied.

The merit of one who gives his sister, daughter, or wife to a family-born yogi who is intoxicated with honey (madhu) cannot be calculated, O Lord of Devas—even that which is cast away by the undisciplined, or increased without effort.

O Dear One, Madhu offered the honey to Vīra as provisions for the journey of the world; he protects the ancestral wealth of his family, which is otherwise joined with sinful conduct and excluded from all society, once it has been offered to the Lord of Kula-yogins.
O Beloved, in whatever land a hero dwells who is devoted to the Kula-worship, that land also becomes meritorious.

How much more so for one standing before him? The merit obtained from eating even once at the home of a supreme Kaulika becomes ten millionfold; how much more so when it is eaten by many? That merit is simply beyond calculation. Therefore, with every effort and in all circumstances, at all times, one should be devoted to the Kula-dharma.

One should worship the knower; whether the knowers are themselves knowers or not, as long as the body is maintained, one must observe the conduct of one's social class (*varṇa*) for the sake of liberation from *karma*. Knowledge that is obscured by actions attains equality through knowledge; by that alone, one is liberated by Śiva.
Therefore, one should perform blameless actions; one should not perform blameworthy actions. O beloved of the gods, how could one who desires fruits in this world or the next be dear to the gods?
It is impossible for one who possesses a body to renounce all actions; rather, he who renounces the fruit of action is a true renunciant.

It is said: "He who acts after having cast aside the sense of 'I'—thinking that it is the instruments which engage in their respective functions—is not tainted. Actions performed immediately after the attainment of knowledge do not touch the knower of reality, just as water does not touch a lotus leaf."

Just as the meritorious and non-meritorious actions of one established in reality go to destruction and do not smear him, so it is with the wind of his continuous practice; O Beloved, he who has attained innate bliss,
who delights in the knowledge of reality, and who is free from all conceptual constructions— he is a wise man whose karma [is thus exhausted].

One should abandon the ritualistic path (karmakāṇḍa) which has been discarded in vain by unwise men; those heretics who consider themselves wise fall into hell, my dear. Just as a tree, having attained its fruit, casts off its flowers without longing, so too the yogi, having attained the ultimate reality (tattva), should abandon all action.

Neither by ten thousand horse-sacrifices nor by ten thousand killings of Brahmins do those upon whose hearts the Brahman resides become stained by merit or sin. Whatever actions exist on earth resulting from the tongue or the organ of generation—
what will he who has renounced the tongue and the organ of generation do with such action?

Thus has been told in brief, O Kuleśāni, a certain yoga characterized by the Lord of Yogis; what more do you wish to hear? Thus ends the section on Kulayoga and other topics in the fifth chapter of the *Śrī Kulārṇava*, the great secret compendium of one hundred thousand verses.

This ninth chapter, titled "The Place," is the weapon consisting of the water for worship, rinsing the mouth, and washing the feet; he himself is the commander-in-chief, the authority over both [the internal and external]; this absolute devotion to his feet is the banner; "O Durgā! is the sound of his kettledrum at the time of victory. Śrī Du...

Salutations to the Goddess in the Ocean of Kula. Internally a Kaula, externally a Śaiva, and among the people a Vaiṣṇava—one should well-guard the Kaula [teaching], O Goddess, like the water inside a coconut fruit.
One should always and with great effort conceal the entire Kula-dharma and so forth in all circumstances.
The Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas are like the child of a mother’s paramour—obvious to all;
the sciences of Shaivism are like a courtesan; but this Kaulika knowledge is like a guarded family wife.
The deities bestow grace upon those who keep it secret; they grant the fulfillment of desires, yet they destroy [those who reveal it].

Those who are illuminators, who know the Kula scriptures of the Lord of Kula, and who are devoted to the Kula worship—those who serve you in secret remain in your presence. A wise man should reveal the Guru but should guard the mantra with effort; through revealing what is not to be revealed, one's spiritual attainment perishes.

O Long-lived One, one who has fallen away from all conduct should take refuge in family conduct; one who has fallen away from family conduct shall go to the Raurava hell. O Lord of Gods, while atonement is seen in the scriptures even for those who have committed great sins, no atonement is seen for one who has fallen from family conduct.
O beloved, if one does not protect the vow by relying on the family dharma (kuladharma) at any time, for that sinner who acts according to his own whims, there shall be calamity,
misfortune, disease, poverty, strife, fear, and the wrath of the Yoginīs due to his transgression.

O Kuleśvarī, by observing proper conduct at every step, the truth of the fulfillment of the command (*ājñāsiddhi*) will arise; neither consecration (*abhiṣeka*), nor mantra, nor the study of scriptures, and so forth, is the cause of the family path (*kulamārga*). Even one of bad character, if he should perform [this] even once with devotion—
Even other twice-born ones obtain the merit of family worship along with the fire-oblation; how much more so others?

Therefore, with every effort, in all circumstances, and at all times, one should be devoted to the worship of the family for the sake of attaining desired fruits. Sacrifice is superior to family worship, and [the fruit of] family worship and the like is supreme.

The sacred ford (tīrtha) is superior to the worship of one's lineage; austerity (tapas) consists of the worship of one's lineage and so forth; charity (dāna) consists of the worship of one's lineage and so forth; ritual action (kriyā) is superior to the worship of one's lineage; knowledge (jñāna) is superior to the worship of one's lineage; happiness (sukha) consists of the worship of one's lineage and so forth; dharma is superior to the worship of one's lineage; and the fruit (phala) is superior to the worship of one's lineage.
Meditation superior to the worship of one's clan, greatness superior to the worship of one's clan,
yoga superior to the worship of one's clan, destiny superior to the worship of one's clan, fortune superior to the worship of one's clan, and worship beginning with the worship of one's clan—
there is none, there is truly none, there is none at all, O Mistress of the Kula! I swear by you.

O Pārvatī, listen to this secret that has never been told before: he who performs the worship of the Kula according to the path prescribed in the Vedas and Śāstras shall attain a station near Me by that very rule; it shall not be otherwise. This is the truth, this is the truth, the truth, the truth—there is no doubt. [This applies even] on one's own ground, in any direction, or in water.
O Beloved, the thousand million yoginīs who move through all the mountains, forests, and lakes— led by Tārā and shining like the sun— are appointed to protect the lineage of Mahādevī;
every single day, on the mountain, in the water, and in the forest, they behold [the practitioner] through the very practice of easy worship.
If unworshipped, they destroy those who desire worldly gain; but if worshipped, they protect them.

They destroy those who are devoted to the guru, who follow right conduct, and who are ever-auspicious in their adherence to the dharma of the guru, yet they do not destroy those who are devoid of devotion, of evil conduct, or who are merely outwardly illuminating [the path]. Thus it is proclaimed in the Kulārṇava.
Then the illustrious Lord said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare that which you ask of me; by the mere hearing of it, a person is liberated from the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
There exists the Supreme Deity, the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is Śiva—partless, omniscient, and all-pervading."

The Creator is the Lord of all, stainless, immutable, self-luminous, without beginning or end, formless, higher than the highest, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda). Those known as individual souls (jīvas) are His portions, accompanied by great effort, like sparks from a fire; indeed, they are all possessed of limiting adjuncts (upādhis).
