Constrained by their own beginningless karmas— which bestow pleasure and pain— and by their merits and demerits, those of deluded minds attain in every birth a subtle *liṅga-śarīra* (subtle body) born of karma, consisting of the various physical forms, lifespan, and objects of experience.

O Beloved, until their liberation from that [state], they remain inexhaustible: the stationary beings, those who move in succession, the commanded ones, the bound souls (paśus), the birds, and human beings;

likewise the celestial beings (tridaśas) and the inhabitants of the earth. Having assumed fourfold bodies by the thousands and tens of thousands through their well-performed deeds, their liberation occurs according to the sequence.

If one becomes a human being yet remains ignorant, one will not attain liberation; among the eighty-four lakh bodies of embodied beings, true knowledge of reality is not obtained anywhere else except in a human form.
O Pārvatī, even after thousands upon thousands of births in this world, it may happen only once—

A living being attains human birth through the accumulation of merit; yet, if one does not restrain oneself from what is harmful, who else can be a benefactor? Therefore, the self alone is considered the savior of the self.
He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here, having gone there...

What will one afflicted by disease do when the medicine has been administered? As long as this body remains, so long should you practice the Truth. What foolish person would descend into a well while his house is ablaze? Prosperity is like a dream; youth is like a flower; and life is like a flash of lightning.
The lifespan of even a wheel-turning monarch is but a moment; for one who knows this, there should be steadfastness.
What is to be done tomorrow must be done today, and what belongs to the afternoon must be done in the forenoon. Death does not wait to see whether one’s work is finished or unfinished.
[Even] the hosts of deities such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, and the multitudes of living beings—all [must fulfill] their hope...

One should practice what is beneficial for those who will follow one; just as a living leech moves from one blade of grass to another, so does the soul enter another body after leaving the previous one. Having attained a subsequent body, it abandons the former body, just as childhood, youth, and old age are followed by other states of the body; such is the attainment of another body.
One who has come from house to house as it were, being free from attachment, shall attain liberation; for all defects are born of attachment.

O beloved, even a man of knowledge falls low because of attachment, let alone one who does not know the Self. Attachment must be abandoned with one's whole being, yet it cannot be abandoned [entirely]; therefore, one should associate with the virtuous, for association with the virtuous is beneficial.

"Suffering is indeed the root of all remedies, for he who possesses it is miserable; O beloved, he by whom that [suffering] has been abandoned is happy, and no other. Since this entire world-process consists of suffering in its beginning, middle, and end, therefore, having completely renounced saṃsāra and being established in reality, become happy."
Even one who is firmly bound by nooses made of *tāla* and *udumbara* wood is released; however, one who is attached to women, wealth, and the like is never released.
Just as a fish greedy for meat does not see the iron hook, so too a person greedy for pleasure does not see this affliction. Sleep—

Fear, sexual intercourse, and laughter are common to all living beings; O Dear One, a human being is said to be one who possesses knowledge, while one devoid of knowledge is a beast. O Dear One, at dawn humans are afflicted by excrement and urine, at midday by hunger and thirst, and at night by passion and sleep.

Alas! All human beings, deluded by ignorance, are devoted only to their own bodies, wealth, wives, and so forth; they are born and they die. O Parvati, although all human beings are devoted to the conduct prescribed for their respective castes and stages of life, they do not know the Supreme Brahman and perish in vain through mere desire.
Men who are satisfied with the ritualistic portion of the Vedas, deluded by mantras, ritual services, fire offerings,
and elaborate sacrifices, and by restrictive vows such as eating but one meal a day that wither the body—
these fools, bewildered by Your Māyā, desire the Unmanifest (the Absolute) merely through the mortification of the body.
The speech of the undiscerning is like a release of arrows; from the striking of a nest, alas, even the birds die!

One should abandon like an outcaste that person who is attached to the pleasures of worldly existence yet claims, "I am a knower of Brahman," having fallen away from both ritual action and the realization of Brahman—such a person whose shame has vanished upon seeing the forest as equal to their own home.

O Goddess, do those who wander naked, such as the followers of the *Gardabha* sect, become yogis? Do they subsist constantly on grass, leaves, and water, dwelling perpetually in the forest? O Supreme Sovereign, do deer and other wild animals become yogis? Are pigeons, stone-eaters, and *cātaka* birds [yogis]?

Do those yogis who do not drink the water of the earth become [liberated]? O Beloved, do pigs and other such creatures—who endure cold, wind, and heat, and for whom edible and inedible food are the same—become knowers of truth? For even frogs and fish dwell upon the banks of the Gaṅgā from birth until death. Do they therefore become wise?
O Mistress of Kula, what do those who are not joined to the [true] path gain from that? Divine powers and the like are merely actions that cause the world to be pleased;

the direct cause of liberation is the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna). O Dear One, the bound souls (paśus) have fallen into the great well of the six systems of philosophy (ṣaddarśana); they do not know the Supreme Self.

Bound by the fetters of worldly existence, they study the Vedas and Shastras and debate with one another, yet they do not know the supreme reality, just as one born blind cannot perceive the taste of sugar.
O Goddess, for one devoid of wisdom, study is like a mirror for a blind man; but for the wise, the scripture is [like a lamp].

The causes of your knowledge are the Vedas and many other scriptures, yet they present millions of obstacles to a short lifespan; therefore, one should discern the essence, just as a swan extracts milk from water. Having practiced all the scriptures and known the ultimate reality, the wise man discards them like straw.

One who seeks the ultimate goal should abandon all scriptures; just as one satisfied by nectar has no need for food, so too, O Lord, one who knows the truth has no need for scripture. Liberation does not come from the study of the Vedas nor even from the recitation of treatises; indeed, liberation comes from knowledge alone.
O Vīramanditā, for one [liberated], there are no stages of life (*āśrama*) as a cause for liberation, nor are philosophical systems (*darśana*) the cause;

likewise, all scriptures are not the cause. Knowledge alone is indeed the cause. For non-duality (*advaita*) is declared to be Śiva, devoid of the exertion of ritual action (*kriyā-āyāsa*), and it is attained through the thunderbolt of the Guru (*guruvajra*).
Therefore, some desire non-duality through millions of scriptural traditions, while others desire duality;

they do not know my true nature, which is devoid of both duality and non-duality. For one who possesses the sense of "mine" there is bondage and liberation, yet for one who is free from "mine," there is neither; it is the creature who possesses the notion of "mine" that is bound.
As long as this [ego] shines forth through karma and the like, so long does the latent tendency for saṃsāra persist;

as long as there is fickleness of the senses, how can there be talk of reality? As long as there is identification with the body and the sense of "mine," and as long as there is no compassion for the Guru...
As long as there is the influence of effort, as long as there is the conceptualization of mental constructs,
and as long as there is no steadiness of the mind, how can there be talk of reality?
As long as there is austerity, vows, pilgrimage sites, recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, as well as discourses on the Vedas, Shastras, and Agamas— how can there be talk of reality?

Therefore, O Goddess, if one desires one's own perfection, one should at all times and in all circumstances strive with every effort to be devoted to Bhava until one finds the ultimate reality; for He is the shade for those scorched by the affliction of the three-fold suffering, and He is the source of dharma, knowledge, deep sleep, and the fruit of the heavenly world.
"One should take refuge in the tree of liberation"— thus, in the *Śrī Kulārṇava*, the great secret, the supreme among all scriptures,

in the fifth section (*pañcamakhaṇḍa*) of the *Ūrdhvāmnāyatantra* within the compendium of one hundred thousand verses (*lakṣagrantha*) along with its supplements (*sapādala*), in the first chapter (*ullāsa*) titled "The Description of the Abiding of the Living Soul" (*jīvasthitikathana*), there are some verses. *Oṃ namaḥ paradevāya*.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving the entire earth to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
that same fruit is obtained in the worship of the Kaulika.
[The fruit] of thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, when performed, [is attained there].

The fruit that one obtains from worshipping the Kaulika is equal to the fruit obtained by giving gold as large as Mount Meru to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; the fruit that one would obtain by constructing wells, ponds, and tanks is increased a hundred thousandfold by worshipping the Kaulika.

The worship of that Kaulika [tradition]—he who, devoted to the Kula scriptures, worships the Kaulika, shall go to a terrible hell; this is the truth, there is no doubt. The Lord of Kula should offer the vessel of the heroes (vīrapātra) according to the sequence of seniority, [a vessel] free from impurity and the like.

A wise person should never offer it with one hand, nor should they ever offer it using only a single palm. Then, having prostrated according to the rules, one should bring the vessel for the initiate with both hands to the hero who has been consecrated and is devoted to the family mantra.
Thereafter, the ritual vessel should be brought by both hands. Having paid homage as prescribed...

Otherwise, one would go to hell according to the rule. Then, having placed [the vessel] upon the support, one should fashion the dead [form]. Upon that, the best of practitioners should recite the mantra eight times, having duly performed the libation (tarpaṇa) to the god Ānandabhairava and the venerable Guru Parameśvarī.
One should perform the purification of the tattvas according to the rules and worship the vessel with devotion while offering salutations to one another.

Having performed the purification and other rites with the right hand, one should take the vessel with the left; saying "I shall take," the wise practitioner should then receive permission from the gurus and the sādhakas.

With a concentrated mind, reciting "vāyuṣvasva," and holding a substance weighing one *lakṣa* of *vāṇa*-units in his lotus-like hand, he should meditate upon the sandals of the venerable Guru within the white great orb of nectar;
thereafter, [he should worship] the Goddess residing in the *kanda*, whose form is consciousness.
Having satiated the lineage with a stream of nectar, those who have performed good deeds shine brilliantly throughout the three worlds.

One should drink the supreme nectar-essence by means of sound alone; one should not drink with a single hand, nor should one let even a drop fall upon the lotus-like surface of the earth. One should fill the vessel one-third full, and then fill that vessel completely. It must be provided with a base and should not be moved.

One should place the mudrā within a clean spot, avoiding fish, meat, and the like; one who is not of noble family should not take it. The vessel should be neither too large nor too small, nor broken, nor mixed with impurities, nor filled from a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), nor lacking the fragrance of sandalwood paste.

Without this, one should not partake of that which is endowed with foul-smelling juices; nor indeed should one do so if it is devoid of mantras, provided that the leader of the *kula* is devoted to *dharma*, wealth, and liberation.
Having caused his own *śakti*, a *vīra-śakti*, or one who has received *kula-dīkṣā* to drink first, he should then drink the substance (*dravya*). Thus it is said.
The determination of the scripture: those lowest of men who sit in a circle upon a single seat,
or eat from a single vessel, or even drink from a single cup what has been brought by another—
out of delusion and ignorance, they go to a most terrible hell.

Having finished eating, one should not touch family property with hands still soiled by food remnants; having washed the hands, one should cause the family property to be brought outside. A hero should not offer the nectar from his own vessel even to Bhairava; in such an offering, there would be a loss of siddhi, and she [the Goddess] would become angry.

The yoginī should eat the remains (ucchiṣṭa) of the Guru, the Śakti, and the sons [of the Guru], as well as those of the elder and younger brothers born of the Guru. She should not offer her own remains to women; rather, having reflected well, she should drink the wine—the supreme nectar—which is the remains of the Śakti, and she should chew the remains of the Vīra.
The leader of the family should indeed give his own leftovers to his younger disciples; however, if he gives them out of pride or affection to others, he will become a vessel for calamities.
Within the circle [of the assembly], one should avoid indifference, derision, idle chatter, excessive talk, fear, anger, and contentious debate.

One should worship the Śrīcakra; whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, that which appears within its pericarp at dawn must not be spoken of—this is the command established by Śambhu. One should avoid spitting upon the cakra, as well as the emission of wind (flatus). A practitioner of mantra should never strike one another with the cup. Śa... [text fragment]

That drinking which is done without *kṛtyā*, that drinking which is done without Manu, and that drinking which is devoid of libations (*tarpaṇa*), shall become fruitless. One should never perform libations at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) that is not endowed with purity;
one should know that such libation is fruitless, and the goddess Caṇḍikā becomes enraged.

In the conduct of the ignorant, when one who has drunk wine repeatedly stumbles and falls upon the ground, as many grains of dust as touch his body, for that long a number of years measured by *reṇu* (atoms) he is honored in the world of Brahmā;
yet having drunk again and again, and drinking once more, he falls back to the earth.

Furthermore, by drinking [this] again and again, rebirth no longer exists. Having drunk and embraced one who is intoxicated by the family custom and exalted by youth, one destroys in that very instant the sins accumulated over ten million births.
By drinking again and again and chanting [the mantra], one is liberated along with ten million kinsmen in the world of Brahmā.

One should always dwell in truth—truth, truth, most firmly resolved; there one attains dissolution and shall not fall back into this world again. Now, in the *Mātṛkābhedatantra*, the Goddess said: "I have heard in all the Tantras that there is great merit in the offering of wine, yet the distinction of castes has not been mentioned; [please explain] this now."

Śaṅkara said: "O Pārvatī, there is no doubt that the Brahmin is the lord of all sacrifices. In the great sacrifice of Sītrāmaṇī, the four castes, beginning with the Brahmins, are present; O speaker of pleasant words, the gift given by me grants great liberation to the Brahmin. The Brahmin is the Supreme Lord."

One should perform the drinking of wine and other rites; at that very moment, O Daughter of the Mountain, he is truly, truly Śiva himself— just as water is merged in water, as light in light, as space in a pot, as wind in wind, O Beloved, so too is the drinker of wine.

O beloved of Brahmāṇī, O Daughter of the Mountain, a Brāhmaṇa who practices *nena* (the ritual of intoxication) merges into the Supreme Self; of this there is no doubt. O Goddess, without the drinking of wine, that knowledge is not obtained.
Therefore, indeed, a Brāhmaṇa should always practice the drinking of wine through the recitation of the Mother of the Vedas alone. A Brāhmaṇa [is not truly such] otherwise.
O Goddess born of the Himalayas, when one possesses the knowledge of Brahman, then one is called a Brāhmaṇa. The nectar of the gods is Brahman;
this [alcohol] is merely worldly liquor (*surā*). O Surā, because it consists of mere enjoyment, it is not proclaimed as the divinity of the gods.
One should always employ the three mantras for liberation from the curses of Brahmā and others.

A twice-born man should indeed perform this; for by the mere offering of the oblation, the fire becomes kindled with the essence of Brahman. By the mere release from the curse, she bestows liberation from the wine. Therefore, O Lord of Gods, a Brāhmaṇa may partake of the drink.
He is a Brāhmaṇa, a knower of all the Vedas, a maintainer of the sacred fire, and one who has been initiated; what more need be said, O Goddess?

He is one whose nature consists of the three qualities (*tri-guṇātmaka*). Śrī Caṇḍikā said: "I have heard from your mouth, in the Vedas and Purāṇas, that great liberation is attained through the cause of the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) of Śiva."
"O Lord of the Gods, your discarded flower-offering (nirmālya) is not to be accepted; O All-pervading One, its cause is not to be accepted.
O Mahādeva, bearer of Yoga, why do you speak such a falsehood? Śrī Śaṅkara said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask me of. I shall tell you all of that."
Listen attentively: the soul indeed wanders through eighty-four hundred thousand lakhs [of births], and only then does it become a vessel for liberation.
O Goddess praised by heroes, if great knowledge should arise within this [cycle], then one attains liberation; otherwise, whose wandering would there be?

O Great Goddess, how could one who has previously been born [in such a state] become a vessel for liberation? O Goddess, how could one whose sins are excessive become a vessel for heaven? Therefore, O Maheśānī, I have performed this act of concealment regarding the *nirmālya*.

If heaven and nirvāṇa were not attained through liquor, or if even an outcaste (caṇḍāla) possessed of sin could attain liberation by consuming the remains of an offering (nirmālya), then liberation would indeed be realizable; for one who is Śiva himself, it is not otherwise.
Even if one burdened with great sins (mahāpātaka) drinks [it] for the sake of knowledge...

One shall attain liberation; truly, there is no distinction of caste and the like. O Supreme Goddess, in all castes, nirvāṇa is attained through knowledge. For this reason, O Great Mistress, I have kept this state secret.
Any statement made for the purpose of secrecy, or even for the sake of jest, does not constitute that [true] statement for its intended meaning.
O Supreme Goddess, O Goddess whose domain is Nirvāṇa, liquor is the supreme cause;
without the drinking of liquor, O Goddess, great liberation is not obtained. Caṇḍikā said:
If one dies right there in the Gaṅgā with knowledge, then liberation is attained through the Gaṅgā. And regarding the Gaṅgā’s...

Śaṅkara said: "O Goddess, you are the Supreme Brahman, difficult for others to attain; O Goddess, you are not otherwise. Gaṅgā, who is worshipped by the gods, is but a single sixteenth part of her. In the Nirvāṇatantra, Śrī Śaṅkara said: "Listen, O Goddess."

O beautiful one, I shall proclaim that supreme reality which is exceedingly difficult to attain; having heard it, you must protect it with effort, as if guarding a noble womb. O Goddess, these five principles—liquor, meat, fish, mudrā, and sexual union—are for the sake of liberation and nirvāṇa, and for the attainment of the eightfold sovereign powers.
O Daughter of the Mountain, supreme liberation is attained through the drinking of wine; by the mere eating of meat, one becomes Nārāyaṇa himself;
by the mere eating of fish, Kālī becomes manifest;
by the mere practice of the *mudrās*, he who assumes the form of Viṣṇu becomes worthy of worship; and by sexual union, [one attains] greatness.
O Goddess of the gods, there is no doubt that the yogi is incomparable; this was previously told by me in other births.
O Goddess of the gods, its majesty was also previously told by me; this knowledge of reality is the absolute cause of liberation and nirvāṇa. [In this] one place are the five principles (tattvas).
Wherever this union occurs, there I go; therefore, O people, you are always equal to me.
That woman is the form of Kālikā, and in her, the nectar dissolves. Those men who are of virtuous form and devoted to the knowledge of reality are declared to be liberated while living (jīvanmukta).

O Supreme Goddess, those who are of the nature of Brahman and not otherwise, having been assigned to the great liberation such as *sāyujya* among the three castes and so forth, and being devoted to the supreme reality, O Parameśānī, the Brāhmaṇa— truly, truly, again truly— merges into the Supreme Tattva, just as water merges into water.

O Supreme Goddess, in that same way, one dissolves into the practice of the principles (tattva) and dissolves into the Supreme Self. Thus, O beloved, I have told you this knowledge of the principles which bestows liberation;
by the grace of which knowledge, the attainment of liberation occurs without a doubt, just as there can be no existence without the earth.
O beloved, just as there can never be a cause for the cessation of thirst without water,
nor a destroyer of darkness without the sun; and just as nothing whatsoever can be cooked without fire, nor [anything produced] without the moon.

O Queen of the Gods, a rain of nectar does not arise without the mother’s womb; O Beloved, birth indeed does not occur otherwise. Therefore, O Great Goddess, protect [this] with effort. Endowed with divine disposition, O Goddess, one should practice the knowledge of reality; likewise, one endowed with the heroic disposition...

O sinless one, the reality of Nāṃca should always be served; one should not do so in the abode of a beast, nor within the range of a beast's knowledge, nor in the vicinity of a beast, nor within the range of a beast's sight. Otherwise, by the mere sight of a bird or an insect, one should certainly not perform it; in that very place, one may fulfill one's desire.

There is no failure where one worships the Cakra; he who performs the worship of the Śrīcakra becomes a protector of the world, imperishable, and obtains the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices—that same fruit is obtained from the Kaulika worship. [Likewise] from wells, ponds, and tanks...
Whatever fruit one might obtain by giving [such a gift], if one were to worship the Cakra, that fruit would be multiplied ten millionfold.
O Goddess, if one worships the Cakra, it becomes equal to Mount Meru; it is like the ocean and its islands, and the flower is like Meru itself. It resides in the center of that, O Goddess.

A man endowed with divine intellect should worship [the reflection] with the thought that it is Śiva, and he should avoid delusion in that regard. Just as one perceives the reflection of the sun in water, so too does the sun appear in the waters of the Gaṅgā;
yet, in water that is not pure, the sun is likewise seen. There is no fault in the sun.
O Supreme Goddess, just as the sun alone remains established [in the sky], so too there is no defect for the practitioner;
merely by the propitiation of the mantra, he becomes its very self and absorbed in it. Therefore, O Great Goddess, there is no defect in the semen; the semen is pure.

The supreme Śakti is indeed the cause of liberation. If one makes such a woman—who is of diverse forms—possess all-knowing wisdom, he will be devoid of wealth and sons and becomes a Caṇḍāla; it is not otherwise.
Thus, O beloved, I have told you the knowledge of reality that bestows liberation for those whose bodies [are purified].
Those in whose bodies the knowledge of the reality of Maheśāna has been proclaimed by me—that knowledge which grants liberation—they never again enter the womb of a mother;
those men are declared to be liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and are of the very nature of Śiva. Purāṇa.
O Pārvatī, when the nectar of my feet shines forth, one may count the multitude of gods,
humans, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras anywhere; O auspicious one, one may always count the wind, for from the moment of the solar eclipse—

No other time is praised as the supreme moment, O Supreme Lord, for [the worship of] the embodied Brahman during the eclipses of the moon and sun; even if a mortal were to abandon all merit, by [failing to worship then], he becomes a worm in excrement. [This is known through] knowledge.
In the glorious third chapter of the *Trepañcama*, it is stated that even Māyā is to be known as an obstacle on the path of liberation.

O Lord of the twice-born, she is the sustainer of the world who bestows liberation; she is the formless Śakti, eternal, of the nature of Brahman, supportless, and the source of the single digit (*ekakalā*).

For the sake of attaining the goal, one should always contemplate the Guru, Śiva, and likewise the Goddess as one through the practice of the Samayācāra-tantra. One should cultivate the knowledge: "I am indeed Śiva alone.
The individual soul (jīva) is Śiva; Śiva is the individual soul; that individual soul is the absolute (kevala).

Śiva is always bound by the fetters, while Sadāśiva is always free from the fetters. Having become eternally one with Śiva, one should perform the five mudrās and so forth; seeing everything as consisting of Brahman, one is not defiled by faults, whether they arise from delusion or even from desire. Whoever [acts thus]...
He who persists in this [prohibited conduct] is the lowest of practitioners and will certainly become a denizen of hell;

he shall be censured in this world and go to hell in the next. Listen, O beloved, to the twofold practice distinguished by the moist and the dry: the "moist" practice (*ārdra-ācāra*) is to be understood as that which begins with the letter *ma*.

Joined with the five *rai*s and devoid of the five *makāra*s, it is proclaimed as the practice of the dry (*śuṣka-ācāra*). O Goddess, in the Kali age, the practice of the moist (*ārdrā-ācāra*) is especially proclaimed. O Mistress of the Gods, within the six traditions (*ṣaḍāmnāya*) and various tantras, the deities are distinguished by their respective divisions of *vidyā* and *mantra*.

In the Kali age, those who are moistened by devotion shall attain victory through meditation upon her; they shall behold the wife of Śiva, Siddhā, who holds a beautiful noose and the Aṅkuśa in her palms, who is Śāṃbhavī, the bestower of the fruits desired by her devotees,
the fortunate one who severs the bonds of saṃsāra, and who arose from the churning of the ocean of nectar.

I bow to Suvijayā, who delights in the play of aesthetic flavors (rasa) and consciousness, the supreme sandal for the propitiation of Vīra, and the enchantress of the world; she who is the great courtesan hidden within the Tantra,
the great courtesan of the Kula, the highly exalted one, the swift courtesan, the divine courtesan, and the Brahman-courtesan— thus sevenfold.

In this world, she who is protected by shame, yet devoid of shame and afflicted by passion, and who resorts to a master like a beast, is proclaimed a *guptaveśyā* (protected courtesan). She who is born of noble lineage (*kulajā*) and belongs to a noble family (*kulaveśyā*) is proclaimed a *mahāveśyā* (great courtesan). A *mahāveśyā* is the mistress of the family, acting according to her own will.

The naked woman (Digambarī), the family courtesan (Kulaveśyā), the noble lady (Kulīnā), the wife of a hero (Vīrapatnī), and the Mistress of the Family (Kuleśvarī) are renowned as Mahodayā. Because she moves in reverse at her own will like a king, she is celebrated as Rājaveśyā; having united with Śiva in the Cakra, she is devoted to recitation and worship.

She who is known as the celestial courtesan (devaveśyā), worshipped in the three worlds, having united with Śiva in the wheel (cakra) and performed the recitation (japa), should perform the rite of purification (cātana). She should converse about the vulva and the phallus (bhaga-liṅga-kathā) and worship [him] again and again; if she is of such a lineage, she is a brahmin courtesan (brahmaveśyā).
These names are proclaimed as belonging to the divine power (divya-śakti) and the sovereign power (īśvara-śakti);

these names are also proclaimed for those born from the four castes. Because she sports like a courtesan (veśyā), she is therefore proclaimed a *veśyā*; all [of them] are born from the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṅkara*).

Those proclaimed as courtesans who have entered the path of the Kula are indeed givers of liberation from the state of a courtesan. This includes kissing and embracing, the display of the body of sexual union,
addressing them at the three junctions of the day, the recitation of the names of the vulva and the phallus, and the act of biting during the limbs of the recitation of the courtesans' mantras.
A courtesan should not engage in long-term union with anyone other than her designated partner (japāṅga), who is presented by the *kareṇu* (the keeper).

She should perform the ritual service (*japāṅga*) daily, rejoicing together with her own [spiritual] Śivas. At night, she herself should recite the mantra upon the yantra through the yoga of Śiva. For courtesans, however, the mere recitation of the mantra constitutes the *puraścaraṇa*.

By reciting the mantra in reverse, one becomes Kālī herself; of this there is no doubt. O Dear One, for women, the accomplishment of the mantra occurs through reverse sexual union (*viparītarata*). By reciting the mantra during reverse sexual union, one shall obtain all prosperity. By reciting the mantra during reverse sexual union, one shall proceed to the state of Nirvāṇa.
Having recited the mantra of the reverse-union (*viparītarata*), one should dwell firmly like Kālī;

for Kālī is the reverse-union, she who extends the reverse, and she whose inhalation and exhalation are reversed—of this there is no doubt. Through the *yoṣidvidyā*, the reverse-union is accomplished.
A prostitute who, even without wealth, is possessed by the passion for perverse pleasure and is honored in the three worlds—

having given a firm embrace and kissed him again and again, she should display her skill with side-glances; such a woman is called a *Kaulikī* (a Kaula consort), and this is the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) of that kind.

O Mistress of the Kula, such is the prostitute; O Dear One, she may be a non-prostitute or a wanton woman (*kulaṭā*). O Goddess, through union with a wanton woman, one shall go to the Raurava hell. A prostitute becomes a *vīra-śakti*; she is praised for the accomplishment of one's own spiritual practice (*puraścaryā*).

In the practice of the Kula, one should employ a courtesan; she who is united with the Śivaliṅga is called a virtuous woman (sādhvī), she who is united with the Śivaliṅga is called a chaste wife (satī), and she who is united with the Śivaliṅga is celebrated as a courtesan (veśyā). Furthermore, the womb is the mother who gives birth, and the liṅga is the father who begets.

The state of death and the state of the father—contemplating both of these is the form of the Liṅga; Mahākāla is the form of the Liṅga and Kālikā is the form of the Yoni. Their union is the supreme fortune; their union is the supreme greatness. Their union is the supreme dharma; their union is the supreme bliss.
She who performs the worship of Śiva without having entered into the state of absorption (*āveśa*) in her own Bhairava shall dwell in the terrible Raurava hell until the dissolution of all beings.
He who does not even mentally recollect his own Vīra-Bhairava goes to hell; he is afflicted by great diseases and suffers defeat. Do not [neglect this].

O Mistress of the Kula of Paśu-veśyās, a veśyā who does not resort to heroes goes to hell; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. O fair-complexioned one, whether out of lust, greed, or for the sake of wealth, a veśyā who has fallen into the company of paśus shall go to the Raurava hell. Nānā...

One who resorts to heroines, courtesans, or those devoted to the company of cattle must be avoided with great effort in the ritual practice of the *nakula-sādhana*; if one should employ such persons, there will be a loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Furthermore, in the worship of the fallen *veśyā* lineage, there shall be disease, sorrow, and the loss of wealth at every moment.

Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in one's own Śivā; one should perform recitation, worship, and other rites directed toward one's own Śivā, who is like a courtesan. Blooming with desire, ever eager for dalliance, the courtesan Kālikā bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
The cremation ground (pitṛbhūmi) is declared to be the bearer of form (rūpadhāriṇī), where Śiva always dwells;
for just as Śiva is to be known as auspicious (śivā), so too is he known as the bearer of the form of the liṅga.
The place of Śiva is the place of the cremation ground (śmaśāna), and the cremation ground is the house of those born of the Kula.

On the eighth and fourteenth days of both lunar fortnights, one who does not worship with the *śmaśāna* [mantra] would be like a mere beast; however, by whomsoever that *yaṃtra* is worshipped, all *yaṃtras* are worshipped. Having fully worshipped and recited [the mantra] there, one shall proceed to the state of *nirvāṇa*. [Regarding] the Mothers...

Having offered the mouth of the father into the eternal Kālī, one, liberated from all sins, shall proceed to the state of Nirvāṇa. Ritual action arises from the Vedas, and through ritual action bondage comes to be; therefore, having abandoned Vedic ritual, one should always remain devoted to the Suratas.
Śambhu, the husband mentioned in the Āgamas, the Guru, the husband mentioned in the Āgamas,
the husband of one born of a noble family (kulajā), and the married husband—
there is no fault in abandoning these husbands during the worship of the Kula, provided one does not abandon a married husband who is [otherwise] fit.

One should not abandon the rites prescribed in the Vedas; Śiva is the Lord of the masters taught in the Āgamas, and the sciences of the Siddhas do not succeed without the Lord of the masters taught in the Āgamas. O Goddess, the Lord of the masters taught in the Āgamas is the bestower of liberation upon women.

A woman of noble family (*kulajā*) should not worship Kālī without her husband as prescribed in the scriptures; however, if her husband has fallen from his status, she may perform the rite of choosing a new one. In that case, she becomes a "secret courtesan" (*guptaveśyā*). A woman of noble family who acts without her husband becomes a secret courtesan on the path of the *Kula*. She alone becomes a secret courtesan when she is devoted to the *Kula* path.

There is no doubt that for those women who have entered the path of their family, once they are liberated, their lineage becomes like the Lord of the Gods (Indra), and they shall become joyful; or else, even if they have departed with supreme speed, they shall become noble-born at the time of the emission of semen.
Know that, O Pārvatī, its cessation is Mahākāla for those entering the Kula path;
at the time of the emission of semen,
the noble woman (Kulīnā) should inform the practitioner, and he should recite the mantra without distraction as an adjunct to the recitation during the emission of semen.

At the time of sexual union, whether with the body or even with the mind, one should disclose it to a woman of noble family through the sequence of breaking the limbs; by signaling the time for the emission of semen,
one should [worship] the goddess Kālikā and Mahākāla with the limbs of recitation during that time.

"O noble one, you have deluded me with the guise of Brahmanism; this is the fruit of but little austerity, attained at the end of many births—Brahmanism has been made a mere livelihood for you. If there were any nature whatsoever on the face of the earth equal to yours, it would not be so, nor would it be equal to that [of true Brahmanism]."

She who exists throughout the three worlds is Kālī, who is unerring even when afflicted by the passion of love; Śiva is her Mahākāla—this is the truth, the absolute truth, there is no doubt. When she, Kālī, reaches sixteen years of age, she becomes intent on valorous prowess.
A woman of fifteen years is Rātārā, one of fourteen years is Sundarī, one of thirteen years is Unmukhī,
and one of twelve years is Bhairavī. Having accepted such a woman who possesses these qualities,
she becomes the Sovereign of the Family of Brahma-Veśyās, renowned as a Mahāsādhvī (Great Holy Woman).

She is difficult to find in these three worlds—whether in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld—whoever that woman may be who stands before him. And he is the divine husband of them all, a hero, a practitioner (*sādhaka*), and a divine yogi; for when he is a divine hero, he becomes the lord of all women, even though he himself is divine.

One should worship with the spirit of a hero those born of all castes; the secret courtesan (guptaveśyā) and the great courtesan (mahāveśyā) are dear to Ayodhyā and Mathurā; Māyā is the family courtesan (kulaveśyā), Mahī is the compassionate one (dayā);
Kāśī is the royal courtesan (rājaveśyā), and Deva is the divine courtesan (devaveśyā).
Tikā, Dvārāvatī, Brahmaveśyā, Saptaitāmokṣadāyikā, Kulīnā, Bhavati, Sākṣāt Kālī, Tārā, Sarasvatī, Kulīnābhā,
Ravīrādhā, Kulīnā, Chinnamastakā, and the goddess Sundarī are all Kulīnās.
O beloved of the noble Māhiṣamardinī, O noble Bagalāmukhī, O noble Dhūmāvatī, O noble Mātaṅgī,
may there be the noble Annapūrṇā, as well as Tripurā and Tvaritā, [and] the chaste wife.

She is of noble lineage, virtuous, chaste, and most exalted; she is of noble birth and bestows the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of mantras and yantras—of this there is no doubt. She is of noble lineage, a daughter of the gods, and of noble lineage are the hosts of *yoginīs*. She is like Urvaśī, Rati, Rāmā, Tilottamā, and the beauty of the noble clans.

All these daughters of noble families roam throughout the entire earth; though born of noble lineage, they are like courtesans of the family, yet remain devoted to the duties of their clan. Relying upon their husbands like cattle, they are intent on worldly desires and curiosities, following strictly the traditional path of their lineage.

If a woman of noble birth who is a courtesan— eager for amorous play and intent on winning over a hero through her clever and heroic disposition— should abandon her own husband and take refuge with a single hero, she would lead him onto the path of the noble; and having taken refuge in that noble path...
If she has entered upon the path of her family and should become husbandless, she should rely on a single hero.

Whether she be of noble birth or of lowly birth, she is born again in her next life; devoted to the dharma of her family, she is praised, or else, through the dharma of her family, she becomes a parrot or one worthy of worship.

One should not worship a woman who is devoid of the Lord of Maheśa (Śiva). If she is unconquered and worthy of worship according to the sequence of worldly custom, one should abandon her and worship a woman of noble family; by the mere sight of one of noble family, all sin [is destroyed].

Just as the destruction of sin occurs by the mere remembrance of the Gaṅgā, so too may there be such destruction. A woman born of a noble family, though belonging to a lineage of high birth, becomes a great courtesan who bestows the fruits of mantra and tantra; she alone bestows the fruits of all courtesans. And of those *siddhi-vidyās* (accomplished sciences)...

O Kuleśvarī, that very Śakti is especially proclaimed as the "all-courtesan" (*sarvaveśyā*) for those of noble lineage when performing worship within the *akula* tradition; she is the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) for the well-born, and even among all courtesans of low birth, she bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). The protector of the earth should honor those women born of low castes who are prescribed [for marriage]; however, whether he be a student or a householder, he must not worship those who are not so ordained.

One should bring even the most excellent Māyā under control; if one does not perform the desired rites prescribed by the scriptures, then for the pleasure of the God of gods, that [omission] results in bondage to Māyā. Śrī Nārada said: "If merit is performed through knowledge, and impurity through ignorance..."
"O leader of the asuras, by whom would the fruit of those two [actions] be experienced at one time? Śiva said:
At one time there may not be the experience of both merit and sin;
first, a great sin committed may meet its end through merit, and then the experiencer of that merit [arises]."

O best of the twice-born, at the conclusion of his merit, that man shall become the enjoyer of sin; thus he dies through sin, and the experience of those two occurs in succession. Nārada said: One should give up one's life upon being released by Rāma, or death should occur in Kāśī.

O best of gods, for one who dies at Jñānagaṅgā, Puruṣottama, Muktidā, or at any of these three holy places (tīrthas), death is indeed [liberating]. O Lord of Gods, wherever a Brahmin who has taken up the staff (daṇḍa)— whether he be a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) or one who has entered the forest-dwelling stage (vānaprastha)— dies, [there too he attains liberation].
Śiva said: "For other wise ones, O Devaka, who are the enjoyer of impurity? [He replied:

'In a sacred field, at a holy ford, or upon death, as well as by the name of Rāma and others; through the manifestation of a multitude of bodies (kāyavyūha), O twice-born one, liberation occurs in the direction of the staff within the body, and by that very means, destruction [of rebirth] is attained.'"
A knower of the first order does not become a partaker of sinful or defiled karma; for in the most auspicious knowledge, O Brahmin, sin becomes separate from the body and,
circulating in the form of wind, does not touch the one possessed of merit through the yoga of knowledge.

O tiger among the twice-born, he should cause the body of the *liṅga*—which is the body of the Lord of Brahmins—to perish; when that body of the *liṅga* has been destroyed, he dissolves into the All-pervading One after death. Having made himself one with Him through the constant state of "I am He," he should wander about, satisfying his own self.

Seeing everything as consisting of Brahman, a person becomes liberated while living; O twice-born one, his very sins and merits then go to destruction. O best of the twice-born, for him there is truly, truly no rebirth. Thus ends a portion from the second chapter of the Śrī Jñānatanttra.
